qs.q: A 58-year-old woman with post-operative biliary strictures develops recurrent episodes of cholangitis. Which surgical intervention is the most appropriate definitive management for her specific type of stricture?
o: Open common bile duct exploration using a T‑tube
Whipple pancreaticoduodenectomy
Roux‑en‑Y hepaticojejunostomy reconstruction
Endoscopic dilation with stent placement alone
qs.e: Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy is specifically indicated for the management of post-operative biliary strictures. Endoscopic dilation is primarily for other benign strictures.
qs.s: Surgical Jaundice: Obstructive Jaundice, Cholangitis and Biliary: MCQs

qs.q: A 58-year-old woman undergoes successful placement of a self-expanding metal stent across a malignant biliary stricture via a percutaneous route. What is the subsequent management regarding her drainage system?
o: A. Stent must be flushed daily with sterile saline to prevent tissue in-growth
B. Secondary surgical bypass must be performed within 48 hours of placement
C. External drain is capped and eventually removed to allow internal drainage
D. External collection bag must remain attached permanently for electrolyte loss
qs.e: Once internal patency is established with a stent, the external drain is capped and eventually removed, allowing complete internal drainage. Metal stents do not require permanent external collection bags.
qs.s: PTC and Percutaneous Biliary Drainage in Obstructive Jaundice: MCQs

qs.q: A 58-year-old man with unresectable pancreatic cancer undergoes successful percutaneous placement of a self-expanding metal stent across a malignant biliary stricture. What is the primary long-term advantage of a metal stent over a plastic catheter in this setting?
o: Total removal of the need for any future interventions
Prevention of external bile loss and resulting fat malabsorption
Larger diameter yielding longer patency before tumor ingrowth
Reduced rate of immediate post‑procedure bile peritonitis
qs.e: Self-expanding metal stents have a wider caliber, which results in significantly longer patency compared to narrow plastic stents. They do not completely eliminate long-term complications or future interventions.
qs.s: PTC and Percutaneous Biliary Drainage in Obstructive Jaundice: MCQs

qs.q: A 59-year-old man with a malignant biliary stricture undergoes percutaneous biliary drainage. During the procedure, the operator carefully monitors the amount of contrast injected into the biliary tree. What is the primary reason for avoiding excessive contrast injection during cholangiography?
o: Reduce the risk of immediate contrast‑induced nephropathy after the procedure
Prevent precipitation of contrast crystals inside intrahepatic bile ducts
Avoid over‑pressurizing the obstructed ducts and causing bacteremia
Avert permanent chemical injury to hepatocytes lining the canaliculi
qs.e: Over-pressurizing an obstructed, infected biliary tree with excessive contrast can cause cholangiovenous reflux and bacteremia or sepsis. It does not typically cause crystal precipitation or direct hepatocyte necrosis.

qs.q: Among all nonmalignant causes of biliary strictures, what is the most frequent etiology?
o: Complications from radiation therapy
Injury during gallbladder removal surgery
Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis
Blunt trauma to the abdomen
qs.e: Injury to the bile ducts during surgery for gallbladder removal accounts for 80% of nonmalignant biliary strictures. Other noncancerous causes like pancreatitis and gallstones are less common by comparison.

qs.q: What proportion of all biliary strictures are estimated to be malignant in origin?
qs.e: Among biliary strictures, 90% are malignant, with pancreatic cancer being the most common malignant cause. Noncancerous etiologies make up only a small fraction of cases.

qs.q: Which specific cancer is identified as the most common malignant cause of a biliary stricture?
o: Pancreatic cancer
Gallbladder cancer
Hepatocellular cancer
Cholangiocarcinoma
qs.e: Pancreatic cancer is the most common malignant cause of biliary strictures, followed by cancers of the gallbladder, bile duct, liver, and large intestine. Cholangiocarcinoma is a distinct biliary tract tumor but ranks secondary to pancreatic primary involvement in stricture statistics.

qs.q: A 67-year-old man presents with painless jaundice and progressive weight loss. Abdominal imaging demonstrates a malignant biliary stricture. What is the most common malignant cause of this finding?
o: Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma
Extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma
Metastatic colon adenocarcinoma
Hepatocellular carcinoma
qs.e: Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma is the most frequent malignant etiology leading to extrinsic compression and stricturing of the common bile duct. Cholangiocarcinoma and metastases are less common causes of malignant strictures.

ai.title: Biliary Strictures
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Biliary strictures are abnormal narrowings of the extra‑hepatic or intra‑hepatic bile ducts, most often caused by stones, inflammation, or malignancy. They present with jaundice, pruritus, and abdominal pain, and require imaging and, if possible, ERCP or surgery. Early recognition prevents liver failure and cholangiocarcinoma.

sections.p: A biliary stricture is a focal narrowing of a bile duct that impedes flow of bile from the liver to the duodenum. Diagnosis is based on clinical features and imaging that shows a tapered segment with upstream dilatation.
b: Jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, pale stools

t.b: Shows upstream ductal dilatation and a focal narrowing – confirms obstruction but not cause
Non‑invasive imaging of the biliary tree; identifies strictures, stones, and masses
Diagnostic and therapeutic; allows brush cytology, stenting, and stone removal
Total >34 µmol/L (2 mg/dL) suggests significant obstruction; rising trend indicates worsening
>2× upper limit indicates cholestasis; helps differentiate hepatic vs. extrahepatic causes

sections.p: Strictures are staged by length, degree of narrowing, and associated complications. The Bismuth classification is used for hilar strictures, while distal strictures are graded by the length of the narrowed segment.
b: Bismuth I–IV for hilar strictures; I = <1 cm, IV = involves both ducts

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, the hierarchy of causes reflects local disease burden.
b: Chronic cholecystitis leading to post‑cholecystectomy stricture

sections.p: Patients often report a triad of jaundice, pruritus, and abdominal pain. Weight loss and anorexia may signal malignancy.
b: Right upper quadrant pain, especially after fatty meals

sections.p: Start with inexpensive tests; advance to imaging if available.

t.b: Rule out anemia or infection; leukocytosis may suggest cholangitis
Elevated ALP and GGT with normal transaminases indicates cholestasis
Elevated in autoimmune pancreatitis causing stricture
First‑line imaging; shows dilated ducts and possible stones
Preferred when available; delineates anatomy and rule out malignancy
Gold standard for diagnosis and treatment of malignant strictures

sections.p: Urgent referral is required for signs of acute cholangitis or impending liver failure.
b: Fever, chills, right upper quadrant tenderness (Charcot’s triad) – acute cholangitis

t.b: Indicates severe obstruction; risk of hepatic encephalopathy
Coagulopathy from liver dysfunction; increases surgical risk

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, relieve obstruction, and monitor liver function.
b: Endoscopic stenting for benign strictures or palliation of malignancy

t.b: Relieves obstruction; chosen over surgery when anatomy is difficult or patient is unfit for surgery
Used for cholangitis; avoid nephrotoxic drugs in renal impairment
Reduces pruritus by binding bile acids; avoid in severe liver failure

sections.p: Regular imaging and liver function tests are needed to detect recurrence or progression.
b: MRCP every 6–12 months for malignant strictures

sections.p: Conditions that mimic biliary strictures include gallstones, hepatic abscess, and pancreatic pseudocyst.
Normal bilirubin can occur early; ALP may be normal in small strictures; imaging may miss short strictures.
b: Early cholestasis may have normal LFTs; repeat testing if suspicion remains

whenToSeekHelp: Fever with RUQ pain (acute cholangitis), sudden worsening jaundice, signs of hepatic encephalopathy, or bleeding from varices

faq.q: What is the most common cause of biliary strictures in East Africa?
faq.a: Choledocholithiasis secondary to gallstone disease is the most frequent cause.

faq.q: Can a biliary stricture be asymptomatic?
faq.a: Yes, short or mild strictures may be silent until they cause obstruction or complications.

faq.q: Why is ERCP preferred over surgery in many cases?
faq.a: ERCP is less invasive, allows simultaneous diagnosis and treatment, and is safer in patients with comorbidities.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man presents with jaundice and RUQ pain. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct with a focal narrowing. What is the next best step? — ERCP for diagnosis and possible stenting.
A patient with a known pancreatic head tumour develops worsening jaundice. Which imaging modality best defines the extent of biliary involvement? — MRCP.
A child in a malaria-endemic area has painless jaundice. What infectious cause should be considered? — Tuberculous cholangitis or schistosomiasis.
You find a 2‑cm stricture at the hepatic hilum. According to Bismuth classification, what type is this? — Type I.
A patient with a biliary stricture is started on antibiotics for cholangitis. Which drug should be avoided in renal failure? — Nephrotoxic antibiotics such as aminoglycosides.
A patient has a biliary stricture and pruritus unresponsive to cholestyramine. What is the next therapeutic option? — Endoscopic stenting or percutaneous drainage.
